- When sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.7) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–3% for next period.
- When sentiment is bearish (≤0.3) or mixed, model often underestimates; increase forecast by 1–3% to account for mean reversion or short-term rebound.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., +5%+ in 3–5 days), model frequently overshoots in subsequent days; apply a “cool-down” correction: subtract 2–5% from forecast 2–3 days post-spike.
- If sentiment flips sharply from bullish to bearish (e.g., 1.0 → 0.0), model often fails to adjust quickly; reduce forecast by 3–5% in next 3–5 days.
- Model tends to over-predict in early horizon (e.g., 1–3 days ahead) when sentiment is volatile; apply a “lag correction” by subtracting 0.5–1.5% for 1–3 day forecasts.
- When sentiment is neutral or mixed (0.3–0.7), model often fails to capture mean reversion; add a “reversion bias” of -0.5% to -2% to forecast for 5–10 day horizon.
- If model forecast is >10% above recent 7-day average, reduce by 1–2% if sentiment is bearish or mixed; if bullish, hold or slightly increase.
- If model forecast is <10% below recent 7-day average, increase by 1–2% if sentiment is bullish or neutral; if bearish, hold or slightly reduce.
